presentingComplaint: Progressive whole-body swelling for 3 weeks, now with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness for 6 hours
history: A 54-year-old man with no prior renal history developed frothy urine and gradually worsening periorbital puffiness that progressed over three weeks to gross swelling of both legs, the scrotum and the abdomen, with a 9 kg weight gain. Over the last few days his urine output has fallen and he has become increasingly breathless lying flat. This morning he developed abrupt right-sided pleuritic chest pain, acute dyspnea and one episode of hemoptysis. He has type 2 diabetes for 4 years (on metformin) but no known cardiac or liver disease, no alcohol excess, and no recent NSAID use. The combination of a subacute nephrotic-range illness now complicated by an acute thromboembolic event is characteristic of the hypercoagulable state of severe nephrotic syndrome (loss of antithrombin III, hypoalbuminemia), most often seen with membranous nephropathy in adults.
examination: Ill-appearing, tachypneic and mildly hypoxic. Marked periorbital edema, bilateral pitting leg edema to the thighs, scrotal edema and tense ascites with shifting dullness. Reduced air entry and stony dullness at both lung bases (transudative effusions). Right pleural rub audible. JVP not elevated; heart sounds normal with no murmur or S3; no hepatomegaly and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Xanthelasma present. Calves soft and non-tender.

labs.urinalysis: 3+ protein, oval fat bodies and fatty casts, no significant hematuria, bland sediment

imaging: Chest radiograph: bilateral pleural effusions, no consolidation, normal heart size. CT pulmonary angiogram: acute segmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe with a small peripheral infarct. Renal ultrasound with Doppler: normal-sized echogenic kidneys, patent renal veins, gross ascites and bilateral pleural effusions. Echocardiogram: normal LV/RV size and function, no valvular disease (excludes cardiac cause of edema).
microbiology: Not applicable - non-infective. Blood cultures not indicated; afebrile.
differentialDiagnoses: Nephrotic syndrome (membranous nephropathy) with anasarca and nephrotic-associated pulmonary embolism
Congestive heart failure with fluid overload
Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and hypoalbuminemia
finalDiagnosis: Severe nephrotic syndrome (adult membranous nephropathy, anti-PLA2R positive) with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, anasarca, AKI and a nephrotic-state complication of acute pulmonary embolism
citations: KDIGO - Glomerular Diseases / Nephrotic Syndrome & Membranous Nephropathy - 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Glomerular Diseases: Nephrotic Syndrome
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective condition; no antibiotics indicated.
contraindications: Avoid aggressive diuresis without attention to intravascular volume in a patient with intravascular depletion and AKI
Anticoagulation for the pulmonary embolism must weigh bleeding risk; heparin efficacy may be reduced by antithrombin III depletion
Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, iodinated contrast where avoidable) given AKI
Do not attribute the edema to heart failure and start high-dose diuretics alone without addressing proteinuria
edgeCases: Nephrotic hypercoagulability can present first as VTE (PE, renal vein or deep vein thrombosis) before the renal diagnosis is made
Serum albumin <2.0-2.5 g/dL (especially membranous nephropathy) markedly raises thrombotic risk
AKI in nephrotic syndrome may reflect intravascular depletion, renal vein thrombosis, or aggressive diuresis rather than intrinsic progression
Pleural effusions and ascites are transudative and can mimic heart failure or cirrhosis despite a normal heart and liver
expectedMaiK: Recognize the triad of nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and edema as nephrotic syndrome, and identify the acute pulmonary embolism as a nephrotic hypercoagulable complication - not a primary cardiac or hepatic cause of the edema.
expectedNextQuestions: Quantify proteinuria (24h urine or spot protein:creatinine ratio) and confirm bland sediment vs nephritic features
Any preceding leg swelling, flank pain or prior clots suggesting renal vein/deep vein thrombosis?
Drug history (NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine), hepatitis B/C, malignancy screen and secondary causes of membranous nephropathy
Assess intravascular volume status to guide diuresis vs volume in the context of AKI
expectedInvestigations: Quantified urine protein (24h or protein:creatinine ratio) and urine microscopy for fatty casts/oval fat bodies
Serum albumin, lipid profile, renal function and electrolytes
CT pulmonary angiogram (done) confirming PE; renal vein Doppler ultrasound
Anti-PLA2R antibody and serologies (HBV, HCV, ANA, complement) for secondary causes
Echocardiography to exclude cardiac cause of edema
regressionAssertions: Top diagnosis must be nephrotic (nephrotic syndrome), not heart_failure or decomp_cirrhosis despite the anasarca and hypoalbuminemia.
Heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema with bland sediment and normal complement must drive the nephrotic classification.
Engine must NOT recommend antibiotics (non-infective; stewardship tier null).
The acute PE must be flagged as a nephrotic-state thromboembolic complication rather than reclassifying the case as primary pe.
AKI and hypoxia must not downgrade recognition of the underlying nephrotic syndrome.
